profile.Goals: daily life in Germany · official exam (Goethe/telc/TestDaF, up to C1) · culture & friends
profile.Support language: English-heavy at A0-A1, fading with level (see SKILL.md)

levels.name: Pre-A1 foundations
levels.desc: Goal: first contact. Sounds, letters, greetings, the first ~50 words, "Was ist das?". Mostly English support. Items are introduced inside conversation, never as a lecture.

items.text: Alphabet A–Z plus ä ö ü ß; say the letter names; spell your own name aloud (buchstabieren)
Vowel length: long vs short (Hüte/Hütte, Beet/Bett) — hear the difference
Umlaut sounds ä, ö, ü (lip rounding for ö and ü)
ch: soft "ich-Laut" vs back "ach-Laut" (ich, Milch / Buch, acht)
sch, and sp-/st- at the start of a word say "schp/scht" (Schule, Sport, Straße)
ei = "eye", ie = long "ee", eu/äu = "oy" (Eis, Brief, neu)
z = "ts", v = "f" (Vater), w = "v", j = "y", s before a vowel = "z" (Sonne)
The German r (back of the throat) and the vowel-like -er/-r ending (Vater, Lehrer)
Final devoicing: -b/-d/-g sound like p/t/k at the end of a word (Hund, Tag, Korb)
Word stress usually on the first syllable; statements fall ↘, yes/no questions rise ↗
Spelling basics: every noun is capitalized; ß vs ss; German is mostly read as it is written
Greetings and goodbyes: Hallo, Guten Morgen/Tag/Abend, Gute Nacht, Tschüss, Auf Wiedersehen, Bis später/morgen
Courtesy: Bitte, Danke, Entschuldigung, Ja, Nein, Kein Problem
Numbers 0–20
About 20 everyday objects, always with article: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch, der Stuhl, die Tür…
Food and drink basics: Wasser, Kaffee, Tee, Milch, Brot, Apfel, Banane, Käse
People: Mann, Frau, Kind, Freund, Freundin, Mutter, Vater
Basic colors (rot, blau, grün, gelb, schwarz, weiß, braun, grau)
A few animals: Hund, Katze, Vogel, Fisch, Pferd
Cognates and Anglizismen: Hotel, Computer, Taxi, Pizza, Handy (watch out: Handy ≠ "handy")
Das ist ein/eine/ein …; Was ist das?
Noun gender der/die/das: every noun is learned WITH its article (and plural when known)
ich bin / du bist / er ist / sie ist / das ist; Ich heiße …
Yes/no questions by flipping the verb: Bist du …? Ist das …?
ein vs kein: Das ist ein Tisch. / Das ist kein Tisch.
Wie geht's? — Gut, danke. / Es geht. / Nicht so gut. Und dir?
Greet and say goodbye (informal and formal)
Say your name and ask for someone's name
Say where you are from (Ich komme aus …) and ask Woher kommst du?
Name things and ask: Was ist das? Wie heißt das auf Deutsch?
Say you do not understand and ask for help: Ich verstehe nicht. Noch einmal, bitte. Langsamer, bitte. Was bedeutet …?
Say yes/no, thank, apologize, ask politely with bitte
Count to 20 and say how old you are
Ask "Wie sagt man … auf Deutsch?" whenever you need a word
Listening: pick out words you already know from a spoken sentence
Read very short signs: Eingang, Ausgang, WC, Bahnhof, Apotheke, Achtung
Learn noun + article (+ plural) as one chunk, never the bare noun
First awareness of du vs Sie
Regional greetings you will hear: Moin (north), Servus / Grüß Gott (south), Gude (Hesse); Hallo works everywhere

levels.name: Breakthrough
levels.desc: Can: understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very simple sentences; introduce yourself; ask and answer basic personal questions. English support is still frequent but fades; Ludwig speaks short, clear German.

items.text: Sentence-level intonation: statements and W-questions fall, yes/no questions rise
Sentence stress on content words; reduced, unstressed little words (ein, und, zu)
Digraphs and clusters in real words: pf, tsch, ng/nk, kn-, qu, ck, tz, chs = ks
Silent h after vowels (sehen, gehen); -ig sounds like "ich"; unstressed -e and -en endings
Numbers that sound alike: 13/30, 14/40, 16/60, 17/70 (dreizehn/dreißig)
Say phone numbers, house numbers, prices, e-mail addresses (at, Punkt, Bindestrich, Unterstrich) aloud
Shadowing: repeat a short line from Ludwig with his rhythm
Personal pronouns (nominative) ich … Sie; choosing du vs Sie
sein and haben, full present tense
Regular verbs in the present: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en
Stems ending in -t/-d/-n (du arbeitest) and -s/-ß/-z (du heißt)
Stem-changing verbs e → i/ie: sprechen, essen, lesen, sehen, nehmen, geben
Stem-changing verbs a → ä: fahren, schlafen, laufen
Main-clause word order, verb in position 2 (Heute spiele ich Fußball)
Yes/no questions (verb first) and W-questions: wer, was, wo, woher, wohin, wann, wie, warum, wie viel, welcher, wie lange
Noun gender and plural patterns (-e, ¨-e, -er, ¨-er, -n/-en, -s, no change); learn noun + article + plural
Definite and indefinite articles in the nominative; ein/kein/mein
Negation: kein (for nouns) vs nicht (everything else) and where nicht stands
Accusative case: den/einen/keinen/meinen; verbs with accusative (haben, brauchen, kaufen, essen, trinken, lesen)
Modal verbs können, müssen, wollen, möchten (+ dürfen, sollen); infinitive goes to the end
Separable verbs in main clauses (aufstehen → Ich stehe um 7 auf; einkaufen, anrufen, mitkommen)
Imperative: du-, ihr- and Sie-form (Komm! Kommt! Kommen Sie!)
Possessive articles mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr (nominative and accusative)
Core prepositions: in, an, auf, bei, mit, nach, von, zu, aus, um, für; am/im/um with time (am Montag, im Juli, um 8 Uhr)
Dative in fixed chunks: mir/dir (Wie geht's dir? Das gefällt mir.), mit dem Bus, in der Stadt, zum/zur
Accusative pronouns: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie (Ich sehe ihn)
es gibt + accusative; impersonal es (Es regnet. Es ist kalt.)
Coordinating conjunctions und, oder, aber, denn, sondern (word order stays the same)
Time expressions and frequency: heute, morgen, gestern, jetzt, immer, oft, manchmal, nie; weekdays, months, dates
Telling the time, informal and official (Viertel nach, halb acht, 14:30); daily schedule
Numbers beyond 100, prices, ordinal numbers for dates (der erste Mai)
gern / lieber / am liebsten; Ich mag …; Ich möchte …
Place and direction adverbs: hier, da, dort, links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten; wo? woher? wohin?
Countries and cities: Ich komme aus …, Ich wohne in …, Ich fahre nach …
Quantities: viel, wenig, ein bisschen, ein Kilo/Liter/Glas/Stück; kein/keine with plurals
Capitalization and punctuation basics: nouns, Sie/Ihr, commas before aber/denn
Recognizing a few Perfekt chunks (Ich habe gut geschlafen. Ich bin müde geworden.)

cats.name: Vocabulary themes (≈ 650 words; Goethe A1 groups included)

items.text: Personal data: Name, Vorname, Nachname, Adresse, Telefonnummer, Alter, Geburtstag, verheiratet, ledig
Countries, nationalities, languages
Family members
Jobs and workplaces (Berufe)
Numbers, prices, currencies, measures and weights
Time: Uhrzeit, Tageszeiten, Wochentage, Monate, Jahreszeiten, Feiertage, Zeitangaben
Colors and clothing
Home, rooms, furniture, household items
Food, drink, meals, restaurant and menu words
Shopping: Geschäfte, Supermarkt, Bäckerei, Preis, bezahlen, bar/mit Karte
Travel and transport: Bahnhof, Bus, Zug, Fahrkarte, Flughafen, Richtung, Himmelsrichtungen
City and orientation: Straße, Platz, Post, Bank, Apotheke, Park, Museum
Daily-routine verbs: aufstehen, frühstücken, arbeiten, schlafen, kochen, lernen
Free time and hobbies: Sport, Musik, Kino, Freunde treffen, Freizeit/Unterhaltung
School and learning: Kurs, Lehrer, Hausaufgabe, Wörterbuch, Schulfächer; classroom instructions
Body and health basics: Kopf, Hand, Bauch, krank, Arzt, Schmerzen
Weather and seasons
Work basics: Arbeit, Büro, Chef, Kollege, Termin
Communication: Telefon, Handy, E-Mail, SMS, Internet, Nachricht
Anglizismen and international words (Job, Team, online, Pizza)
The ~100 most frequent verbs (sein, haben, machen, gehen, kommen, wohnen, heißen, brauchen, fahren, sprechen…)
Frequent adjectives and adverbs: gut, schlecht, groß, klein, teuer, billig, schön, neu, alt, schnell, langsam, richtig, falsch
Question words, frequency adverbs and the first connectors
Introduce yourself and others (name, origin, home town, job, age, family)
Give and ask for personal data: spell your name, give address and phone number, fill in a simple form
Ask and answer simple personal questions (Wie alt bist du? Was machst du? Wo wohnst du?)
Order food and drinks and pay (Ich möchte …, Die Rechnung, bitte; Zusammen oder getrennt?)
Shop: ask for items and prices, quantities, "too expensive", cash or card
Ask for and understand simple directions (Wo ist …? Wie komme ich zum …?)
Tell and ask the time; make simple appointments (Treffen wir uns um …?)
Say what you like and dislike (Ich mag …, Ich esse gern …)
Describe your family, your home and your daily routine in simple sentences
Invite, accept and decline politely (Hast du Lust …? Ja, gern! / Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht.)
Ask for help and clarification (Wie bitte? Wie schreibt man das? Was bedeutet …?)
Basic phone phrases (Hallo, hier ist …; Kann ich bitte … sprechen?)
Write a short note, postcard, SMS or e-mail (30–40 words) with greeting and closing
Buy a ticket and ask departure times (Eine Fahrkarte nach …, Wann fährt …?)
Say how you feel and name basic ailments (Mir ist kalt. Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.)
Understand signs, menus, timetables, short announcements and ads
Thank, apologize, congratulate and wish (Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!)
Talk about the weather (Es regnet. Heute ist es sonnig.)
Everyday reactions: Genau, Stimmt, Klar, Echt?, Super, Schade, Na ja, Alles klar
Short spoken answers instead of full sentences (Kaffee, bitte. — Gern.)
Hesitation sounds: äh, also, mal sehen
Question tags: …, oder? …, ne? (Du kommst morgen, oder?)
Polite formulas: Bitte schön, Danke schön, Gern geschehen, Guten Appetit, Prost, Gleichfalls
Greeting registers: Hallo / Hi / Guten Tag / Tschüss / Auf Wiedersehen / Bis später
Doch as the answer to a negative question (Kommst du nicht? — Doch!)
Softening with mal (Komm mal her. Warte mal.)
du vs Sie in practice (colleagues, shops, strangers, children)
Punctuality and appointments (Termin culture)
Shopping rules: Sonntagsruhe, opening hours, Pfand, bringing your own bag, cash vs card
Bakery and café habits: Brötchen, Kaffee und Kuchen, tipping by rounding up
Public transport basics: tickets, validating, zones, monthly passes
Waste separation (Mülltrennung) and quiet hours (Ruhezeiten)
Table manners and toasts: Guten Appetit, Prost with eye contact
Addresses, floors (Erdgeschoss = ground floor), doorbell names
Listening: follow slow, clear speech on familiar topics; catch numbers, times and names
Reading: signs, short messages, menus; guess cognates
Writing: fill in forms; 3–4 connected sentences about yourself
Strategy phrases: Langsamer, bitte. Noch einmal, bitte. Wie sagt man …?
Dictionary skills: look up gender, plural, separable and irregular verbs
Sprechen: introduce yourself; ask and answer with key words; make and answer simple requests
Schreiben: fill in a form; write a short message
Hören/Lesen: short announcements, messages, signs; matching and true/false tasks
One relaxed practice run of a mini-exam conversation when the level check is due

levels.name: Waystage
levels.desc: Can: handle routine situations with simple direct exchanges; describe people and surroundings; talk about the past. English is mostly used for corrections and rare words; Ludwig speaks normal-slow, clear German with short sentences.

items.text: Reduced endings in speech: -en → "n/m" (haben → "habm"), -e, -er
Stress in separable vs inseparable verbs (ánrufen vs besúchen)
Polite request intonation and sentence melody (Könnten Sie …?)
ö/ü and ch contrasts in minimal pairs (schon/schön, Kuchen/Küche)
Common spelling traps: das/dass, ie/ei, ss/ß, double consonants, capitalized Sie/Ihr
Glottal stop and linking between words (am Anfang, in Ordnung)
Perfekt with haben: regular (gemacht) and common irregular Partizip II forms (gegessen, gesehen, getrunken)
Perfekt with sein: movement and change of state (gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, passiert)
Partizip II of separable (aufgestanden), inseparable (besucht, verstanden) and -ieren verbs (telefoniert)
Präteritum of sein, haben and modal verbs (war, hatte, konnte, musste, wollte, durfte, sollte)
Dative case: dem/der/dem/den + -n, kein-/mein- in the dative
Dative pronouns mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen; verbs with dative (helfen, gefallen, gehören, schmecken, danken, passen)
Verbs with dative + accusative (geben, schenken, zeigen, schicken, erklären); order of two objects
Dative prepositions: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber; contractions zum, zur, beim, vom
Accusative prepositions: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um, bis
Two-way prepositions (an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen): Wo? + dative, Wohin? + accusative
Position verbs: stehen/stellen, liegen/legen, sitzen/setzen, hängen/hängen
Subordinate clauses with weil, dass, wenn, ob: verb at the end, comma
Subordinate clause in first position (Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause): verb–verb collision and inversion
Indirect questions: Ich weiß nicht, wo/ob/wann …
Connecting adverbs deshalb, deswegen, darum, trotzdem (verb stays in position 2)
Reflexive verbs: sich freuen, waschen, treffen, interessieren für, erinnern, entscheiden
Comparative and superlative: -er, am -sten; gut/besser/am besten, gern/lieber/am liebsten, viel/mehr/am meisten; so … wie, als
Adjective endings after definite and indefinite articles in nominative and accusative (der große Tisch, einen großen Tisch)
Konjunktiv II basics: würde + infinitive, hätte, wäre, könnte for polite requests, wishes, advice (Ich hätte gern …, Du solltest …)
Future with werden, and present + time word for the future; werden as a full verb
Indefinite words: man, jemand, niemand, etwas, nichts, alle, viele, einige, jeder, welcher/dieser
Genitive recognition (Annas Buch, das Auto meines Vaters) and the von + dative replacement
Time prepositions and adverbs: vor, nach, seit, bis, ab, von … bis, gegen, während; als vs wenn (simple)
Ordinals, dates, years (am 3. Mai 2024), percent and fractions
Imperative with separable, reflexive and polite forms (Setzen Sie sich! Ruf mich mal an!)
Word order: time before place (gestern im Park), Satzklammer with Perfekt and modals
Negation review: nicht position with Perfekt and modals, noch nicht, nicht mehr, noch nie, kein … mehr
Verbs with prepositions (warten auf, sich freuen auf/über, denken an, sprechen über, fragen nach, Angst vor) and da-/wo-compounds (darauf, worauf)
Possessive articles in all A2 cases; dative of mein/dein
Question forms: Was für ein …? Welcher …? Wem gehört …? Wen/Wem …? Wie oft/lange/viel
wissen vs kennen vs können
Degree words: sehr, ziemlich, zu, ganz, ein bisschen, total, ziemlich
Gender patterns: -ung/-heit/-keit/-schaft are feminine, -chen/-lein neuter, -er persons masculine
lassen (Lass uns gehen. Ich lasse mein Rad reparieren.)
um … zu and zu + infinitive first contact
Health: body parts, doctor, pharmacy, illnesses, symptoms, appointment
Travel: hotel, booking, luggage, flight, train (Gleis, Verspätung, Anschluss, Reservierung)
Housing: flat search, rent, extra costs, deposit, landlord, neighbours, moving
Work: application basics, CV, working hours, salary, interview, colleagues, holiday
Education: school, university, apprenticeship, exam, subject, course
Offices and services: registration, appointment, form, passport/ID, post, bank, account
Shopping in depth: complaint, exchange, size, discount, receipt, online shopping, offer
Restaurant and cooking: menu, dish, tip, starter, recipe, ingredients
Clothing, appearance and character adjectives
Leisure and culture: club, sport, concert, exhibition, cinema, invitation
Media and technology: phone, internet, app, password, social media, TV
Weather and environment: forecast, climate, nature, animals, recycling
Feelings and moods
Relationships: relatives, friends, marriage, children, wedding
Festivals and customs: Weihnachten, Ostern, Silvester, Karneval, Geburtstag
City and traffic: public transport, traffic jam, bike, car, driving licence, roadworks
Sequence and time words: zuerst, dann, danach, später, früher, vorher, schließlich, am Ende
Quantity and comparison: mehr, weniger, genug, zu viel, Prozent, Durchschnitt
About 150 further verbs incl. separable ones (anmelden, abholen, einladen, mitbringen, ausfüllen, vorbereiten)
Opinion and agreement words: meiner Meinung nach, ich finde, einverstanden, dafür, dagegen
Verb + noun collocations (einen Termin machen, Hunger haben, eine Pause machen, die Prüfung bestehen)
Tell about past events (gestern, letztes Wochenende, im Urlaub) using Perfekt
Make, change and cancel plans (Zeit und Ort vereinbaren, absagen, verschieben)
Give reasons and simple explanations (weil, deshalb)
Give opinions, likes and dislikes, agree and disagree simply
Describe people, places, objects, your flat and your town
Compare things, people and options
Give advice and make suggestions (Du solltest …, Wie wäre es mit …?)
Polite requests and offers (Könnten Sie …? Darf ich …? Soll ich …?)
Phone calls: make an appointment, leave a message, spell and repeat information
At the doctor's: describe symptoms, understand advice, buy medicine
Housing: ask about rent and details, report a problem
Offices and services: book an appointment, ask which documents are needed, fill in a form
Shopping complaints and returns (Das ist kaputt. Ich möchte umtauschen.)
Travel: book a room, buy tickets, understand delays and announcements, ask for connections
Write informal and short formal e-mails (Liebe …, Sehr geehrte …, Viele Grüße, Mit freundlichen Grüßen)
Give a one-minute talk about yourself, a hobby or a city
Understand the main points of short texts, voicemails, announcements, simple news
Small talk that keeps going: weather, weekend, work, family, with follow-up questions
React to news and stories (Wie schön! Das tut mir leid. Wirklich?)
Express wishes, hopes and intentions (Ich würde gern …, Ich hoffe, dass …)
Talk about abilities, obligations and permission in the present and past
Reserve a table, order, pay, split the bill
Describe a typical day and past habits (früher)
First modal particles: doch, mal, ja, denn, eben, halt, schon, aber (recognize all, use mal/doch/ja)
Spoken Perfekt vs written Präteritum: speak in Perfekt (except sein/haben/modals)
Spoken reductions: hab, gehn, 'nen/'ne/'n, gibt's, ham wir, haste/biste (recognize)
Discourse markers: also, na ja, genau, eigentlich, übrigens, jedenfalls
Hedging and politeness: vielleicht, eher, irgendwie, ein bisschen
Interjections and reactions: Mensch!, Oh je, Na toll, Schade, Pech gehabt, Klasse, Prima
Natural short replies: Gerne. Kein Ding. Passt. Geht klar. Mach ich. Alles gut.
Leave-takings: Schönen Tag noch! Bis dann! Mach's gut! Schönes Wochenende!
Ways to say "I think": Ich finde, glaube, denke, meine, schätze
Switching from Sie to du (Wir können uns duzen) and texting style (LG, VG, Danke dir!)
Anmeldung (Bürgeramt, registering your address), online appointments, official German basics
Health system basics: Krankenkasse, Hausarzt, Überweisung, Krankschreibung, prescription
Renting: Kaltmiete/Warmmiete, Kaution, Nebenkosten, Mietvertrag, Hausordnung
Holidays and traditions: Weihnachtsmarkt, Silvester, Karneval, Ostern, Tag der Deutschen Einheit
Trains and regional transport: Deutsche Bahn, delays, platforms, reservations
Work culture basics: Feierabend, vacation days, punctuality
School, apprenticeship (dual system) and university overview
Regional variety: dialects, Austria and Switzerland (Grüezi, Servus)
Mealtimes and typical foods (Frühstück, Mittagessen, Abendbrot)
Listening: normal-slow standard speech on familiar topics; phone numbers, times, appointments
Reading: short texts, e-mails, ads, timetables, simple articles; guess from context
Writing: 60–80 word messages with connectors
Speaking: one-minute monologue without falling back to English
Circumlocution: describe a word you do not know (Das Ding, mit dem man …)
Use a learner dictionary (DWDS, Duden) for meaning, gender, plural, examples
Self-correction: notice and repair your own mistakes
Sprechen: questions and answers on key words; talk about a topic; plan something together
Schreiben: a short message and an informal e-mail
Hören/Lesen: short dialogues, messages, ads, timetables
One relaxed practice run before the level check

levels.name: Threshold
levels.desc: Can: cope with most everyday situations; tell experiences and plans; give short reasons for opinions; follow clear standard speech. Ludwig now explains in German by default and switches to English only on request or for tricky rules.

items.text: Natural speed: linking, elision and weak forms (haben wir → "hamwa", eigentlich, vielleicht)
Contrastive stress to show emphasis or contrast (Ich habe NICHT gesagt …)
Pronouncing loanwords and names (Internet, Computer, Ingenieur, Chemie, Restaurant)
Comma rules for Nebensätze and infinitive groups; common spelling confusions (seit/seid, wieder/wider, das/dass)
Reading aloud a paragraph with sentence melody and pauses
Präteritum of regular and common irregular verbs for narration (ging, kam, sah, sagte, war)
Plusquamperfekt (hatte/war + Partizip II) and sequence of past events
Subordinate conjunctions: obwohl, damit, bevor, nachdem, während, seit(dem), bis, sobald, falls, als vs wenn
um … zu and damit (purpose); (an)statt … zu; ohne … zu
Infinitive with zu after verbs, nouns and adjectives (Ich habe vor, … zu …; Es ist wichtig, … zu …)
Relative clauses: nominative, accusative, dative and with prepositions (der Mann, mit dem ich spreche)
Adjective declension in full: all cases, with definite, indefinite and no article
Genitive: articles, names, and prepositions wegen, trotz, während, statt
Passive (Vorgangspassiv) in Präsens, Präteritum and Perfekt; passive with modal verbs; von + dative agent
Konjunktiv II: hätte/wäre/würde/könnte; unreal conditions (Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich …); wishes; polite forms
lassen (reflexive: Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden) and other verb uses
Verbs with prepositions: a broad set with case (sich interessieren für, warten auf, träumen von, diskutieren über, abhängen von)
Pronominal adverbs da(r)-/wo(r)-: darauf, davon, worüber, womit
Two-part connectors: entweder … oder, weder … noch, sowohl … als auch, nicht nur … sondern auch, zwar … aber, einerseits … andererseits
Adverbial connectors: außerdem, trotzdem, deshalb, sonst, dann, also, allerdings, dagegen, deswegen
Word order in the middle field: dative before accusative, pronouns before nouns, time–cause–manner–place (TeKaMoLo)
Reflexive verbs with accusative and dative pronouns (Ich wasche mir die Hände)
n-Deklination (der Junge, den Jungen; der Name, des Namens) and weak masculine nouns
Participles as adjectives (spannende Geschichte, geöffnete Tür) — recognition and simple use
Comparative details: je … desto, immer + comparative, als ob, genauso … wie
Indirect speech with indicative or Konjunktiv II: first steps (Er sagt, dass …)
Futur I for plans and assumptions (Er wird wohl krank sein)
Word formation: noun from verb (-ung, Infinitiv as noun), prefixes un-, miss-, ver-, ent-, be-; -heit, -keit, -lich, -bar
Negation in depth: kein/nicht/nie/niemals/nichts/niemand/nirgends, nicht nur, gar nicht
Indefinite pronouns and quantifiers: irgendein, irgendwo, manche, mehrere, wenige, beide, sämtliche
Impersonal and placeholder es (Es kommt darauf an, dass …; Es gibt …; Es freut mich, dass …)
Verbs with fixed cases and reflexive/idiomatic uses (gefallen, fehlen, auffallen, sich vorstellen)
Numbers, statistics, percentages and trends (steigen, sinken, ein Viertel der …)
Subjective modal verbs: first contact (Er soll krank sein; Sie muss müde sein)

City and country life, consumption and advertising
Family and relationships, generations, conflict and compromise
Feelings and personality: abstract nouns (Angst, Hoffnung, Erfolg, Enttäuschung, Stolz)
Time, causes and consequences: Grund, Folge, Ursache, Wirkung, Voraussetzung
Verbs of speaking and thinking: behaupten, vermuten, bezweifeln, erwähnen, zustimmen
Adjectives with prepositions (stolz auf, zufrieden mit, abhängig von, verantwortlich für)
Nouns with prepositions (Interesse an, Angst vor, Lust auf, Hoffnung auf)

Compare options and make a decision together
Summarize a short text, film, or book plot in your own words
Write a formal e-mail or letter (application, request, complaint, apology) and an informal letter
Write a short forum post with an opinion and reasons (≈ 80–100 words)
Handle phone calls with offices, doctors and service providers
Give a short prepared presentation (2–3 minutes) with structure and visuals
Agree, disagree, hedge, concede (Da hast du recht, aber …; Ich sehe das anders)
Give instructions and explain how something works
Hypothesize and give advice (Wenn ich du wäre, würde ich …)
Report what someone said (simple indirect speech)
Ask follow-up questions and keep a conversation going without long pauses
Complain politely and negotiate a solution
Describe a problem and ask for help or information in everyday situations
Take part in an interview (ask and answer about work, studies, interests)
Understand radio and TV news, weather reports and interviews at moderate speed
Describe feelings, relationships and experiences in more detail
Modal particles in active use: doch, ja, eben, halt, mal, denn, schon, eigentlich, wohl, ruhig
Everyday idioms and set phrases (Daumen drücken, Bahnhof verstehen, Das ist mir Wurst)
Standard German vs colloquial speech (weil + main clause, ne, 'ne, Ich hab, gehste)
Fillers and thinking time (also, ja, na ja, sozusagen, quasi, wie soll ich sagen)
Small talk topics and openers (Und, wie war dein Wochenende?)
Softeners and polite disagreement (Ich würde eher sagen …, Vielleicht sollten wir …)
Regional flavour: how Hessian and other dialects sound (Ei gude wie?), plus where Standard German is used
Understanding fast casual speech: elisions and swallowed endings
Texting and chat style, emojis and abbreviations, voice messages
Associations (Vereine), volunteering and neighbourhood life
Work life: contracts, working time, trial period, works council, notice periods
Bureaucracy: Bürgeramt, Ausländerbehörde, Finanzamt, Krankenkasse, Rundfunkbeitrag
Holidays, regional traditions and food culture

Politics and the federal system (Bund, Länder, Gemeinden), elections basics
Shared flats, rental law basics, noise rules and Hausordnung
German history in broad strokes: division, 1989/90, EU
Relay the key points of a short text or announcement to someone in another language
Pass on specific information from a notice, timetable or letter
Explain a simple graph, form or instructions for others

Reading: articles, letters, instructions; main ideas and details; guess unknown words
Writing: coherent texts of 100–150 words with paragraphs and connectors
Speaking: sustain a conversation of several minutes, repair breakdowns (Wie meinst du das?)
Plan, structure and rehearse a short talk
Use a monolingual dictionary and a corpus (DWDS) for collocations
Self-correction and editing of your own writing

Time management in a full practice run

levels.name: Vantage
levels.desc: Can: understand the main ideas of complex texts; interact with a degree of fluency with native speakers; explain a viewpoint and weigh pros and cons. Ludwig speaks natural German at near-normal speed; English only on request.

items.text: Accent reduction priorities: ach-/ich-Laut, vocalized r, final devoicing, glottal stop, vowel quality in unstressed syllables
Sentence melody for emphasis, irony, doubt, politeness and turn-taking
Connected-speech rhythm: stressed vs unstressed syllables in long sentences
Comma rules in complex sentences (relative clauses, infinitive groups, apposition)
Spelling of loanwords and compound nouns (Zusammen-/Getrenntschreibung)
Konjunktiv I for indirect speech (er sei, sie habe, man sage) and replacement by Konjunktiv II
Konjunktiv II in the past (hätte gemacht, wäre gegangen); unreal past conditions; als ob / als wenn
Conditionals without wenn (Hätte ich Zeit, würde ich …; Sollte es regnen, …)
Passive variants: Zustandspassiv (ist geschlossen), sich lassen + infinitive, sein + zu + infinitive, -bar, -lich
Participial attributes and extended attributes (der gestern veröffentlichte Artikel; das auf dem Tisch liegende Buch)
Nominalization and verbalization (Nominalstil ↔ Verbalstil): Nach der Ankunft = Nachdem wir angekommen sind
Genitive prepositions: aufgrund, infolge, anhand, hinsichtlich, bezüglich, angesichts, mithilfe, innerhalb, außerhalb
Advanced connectors: indem, sodass, falls, sofern, es sei denn, wohingegen, demnach, folglich, dennoch, allerdings
Concessive, causal, consequential, modal, final and temporal clauses: forms and style differences
Subjective vs objective use of modal verbs (Er soll reich sein. Sie muss krank sein. Er dürfte da sein.)
Futur II and assumptions about the past (Er wird es vergessen haben)
Verbs with fixed prepositions (extensive list) and noun/adjective + preposition collocations
Funktionsverbgefüge (in Frage stellen, zur Verfügung stellen, in Betracht ziehen, Rücksicht nehmen)
Relative clauses with was, wo, wer, wohin and with genitive (dessen, deren); relative clauses with prepositions
Adjectives and participles used as nouns (der Angestellte, das Beste, Reisende)
Word formation: compounding, derivation, prefixes ent-, ver-, zer-, miss-, un-, suffixes -bar, -los, -haft, -sam, -ig
Field-of-view word order: variation of the Vorfeld for emphasis and cohesion; Nachfeld
Text cohesion: pronouns, adverbs, repeated reference, connectors (zudem, außerdem, darüber hinaus, folglich)
Verb valency and case government (including genitive verbs: gedenken, bedürfen)
Reduced subordinate clauses with infinitive and participle (Ohne zu zögern, …; Das Ziel vor Augen, …)
Tense sequence in reports and narratives; historical present
Comparison nuances: je … desto/umso, deutlich/erheblich + comparative, am meisten
Statements of probability and attitude: vermutlich, wahrscheinlich, womöglich, offenbar, anscheinend, scheinen zu, drohen zu
Prepositions and cases in time, cause and condition phrases (bei Regen, im Falle, im Laufe, seit, binnen)
Modal particles in writing and the limits of their use

Abstract nouns and nominal phrases typical of formal texts

Idiomatic collocations by topic (Weichen stellen, auf der Kippe stehen, ins Gewicht fallen)
Synonym sets and register: gehen/fortbewegen, bekommen/erhalten, anfangen/beginnen
Prefix and particle verbs with shifting meaning (an-, auf-, aus-, durch-, über-, um-, unter-)
False friends and commonly confused pairs (bekommen/werden, wissen/kennen, scheinbar/anscheinend)
Argue a position with evidence and counter-arguments (Erörterung: pro and contra)
Describe and interpret charts, statistics and trends
Write a formal statement (Stellungnahme), complaint, application with cover letter

Take effective notes and write a minutes-style summary (Protokoll)

Irony, understatement and sarcasm (Na, das hat ja super geklappt.)
Youth slang and trending expressions: recognize, decide when to use
Dialect awareness: Bairisch, Schwäbisch, Sächsisch, Hessisch, Kölsch, Schweizerdeutsch, Österreichisches Deutsch
Politeness strategies and indirectness at work (Hätten Sie vielleicht kurz Zeit?)
Typical collocations and chunks natives rely on
Reduction and informality in speech: no-contraction vs contraction choices by context
Register shifts: formal ↔ informal in the same conversation
German-specific habits: Direktheit, Sachlichkeit, Small-Talk-Grenzen, Feedback culture
Political culture: Koalitionen, Föderalismus, Debattenkultur, Volksentscheide
Workplace norms: hierarchy, Siezen/Duzen, meetings, Mitbestimmung

Austria and Switzerland: vocabulary, institutions and variants

Famous works, authors, films and music every German speaker knows

levels.name: Effective operational proficiency
levels.desc: Can: express yourself fluently and spontaneously; use the language flexibly in social, academic and professional life; understand long, demanding texts and implicit meaning. Ludwig talks like a native friend: natural speed, idioms, irony, regional colour; he corrects style and register, not only grammar.

items.text: Near-native prosody: sentence melody, rhythm, contrastive stress, emotional colouring
Connected speech and reductions at natural speed (haste, kannste, hamma, nich) — produce selectively, understand fully
Remaining accent patterns: ch, r, ü/ö, final devoicing, glottal stop; targeted drills only where they affect clarity
Pronouncing foreign words, names, abbreviations and technical terms
Advanced spelling and punctuation: Getrennt-/Zusammenschreibung, commas in participial and infinitive constructions, Anführungszeichen, Gedankenstrich
Nominal style vs verbal style: choosing deliberately for register
Konjunktiv I and II in all functions, including press and academic reporting; Konjunktiv in indirect questions
Extended participial attributes in dense formal texts, including their unpacking and use
Formal connectors: indessen, mithin, wohingegen, insofern … als, demzufolge, ungeachtet, zumal, nämlich, sprich
Passive alternatives and agentless style (man, sich lassen, sein + zu, -bar, Funktionsverbgefüge)
Modal particles in all functions and their combinations (ja doch, eben doch, halt mal)
Subjective modal verbs and evidential verbs (angeblich, scheinen, sollen, wollen, dürften)
Inversion and fronting for emphasis; Satzklammer variation; Ausklammerung in speech
Complex sentence building: multiple subordinate levels without losing clarity
Ellipsis and reduction in coordinated structures; parallelism
Verbs with genitive and rare cases; archaic and fixed expressions (eingedenk, dessen ungeachtet)
Word formation from Latin and Greek roots; technical and academic vocabulary patterns; abbreviations and acronyms
Tense and aspect nuance in narration, commentary, reports; Präteritum vs Perfekt by medium
Pronominal and referential cohesion in long texts; avoiding repetition
Article, preposition and case choices in fixed phrases and idioms
Quantifiers, degree and stance adverbs for fine nuance (durchaus, keineswegs, schlechterdings, allenfalls, zumindest)
Conditionals, concessive and hypothetical structures in elevated style
Rhetorical devices in German: Parallelismus, Antithese, Ironie, Litotes, rhetorical questions
Historical forms you meet in literature (Präteritum of rare verbs, genitive objects, old spellings)
Academic writing vocabulary: These, Hypothese, Methodik, Ergebnisse, Fazit, Quelle, belegen
Professional and field-specific vocabulary (choose your domain: business, law, tech, medicine, humanities, arts, science)
Politics, economy and international relations at press level
Society, ethics and philosophy: abstract nouns and nuanced adjectives
Law, administration and formal documents (Bescheid, Widerspruch, Rechtsbehelf, Satzung)
Literature and arts: Motiv, Erzählperspektive, Epoche, Rezeption, Kritik
Media analysis: Framing, Berichterstattung, Meinungsmache, Quellenlage
Science and technology: Verfahren, Messung, Korrelation, Kausalität, Gutachten
Idioms, proverbs and fixed expressions across registers
Collocation fields: strong verb-noun-adjective combinations natives use without thinking
Synonym nuance and connotation: sagen/behaupten/betonen/konstatieren, gehen/schreiten/laufen
Colloquial and slang register: when it is right and when it is not
Regional vocabulary: Austrian and Swiss standard variants, regionalisms (Brötchen/Semmel/Schrippe, Tüte/Sackerl)
Anglicisms, Denglisch and the debate around them; German equivalents
Humour vocabulary: Wortspiel, Doppeldeutigkeit, Pointe, Kabarett
Take part effortlessly in any conversation or discussion, including abstract and complex topics
Present a clear, well-structured talk with nuance, emphasis and handling of interruptions
Write clear, detailed, well-structured texts (≥ 250 words) on complex topics: essay, report, review, formal letter
Write a persuasive text (Kommentar, Leserbrief, Stellungnahme) with rhetorical control
Summarize and synthesize several long sources into one text
Analyze a text: structure, argument, style, intent, implicit meaning, attitude
Understand extended speech, even when not clearly structured, and TV/film without effort

Negotiate, persuade, advise, and handle sensitive or confrontational situations tactfully

Chair or moderate a meeting or discussion
Give and receive nuanced feedback and criticism

Native-like idiomatic phrasing instead of word-for-word translation from English

Humour, wordplay, irony and cultural references (Kabarett, Satire, memes)
Dialect understanding and code-switching awareness; when natives use regional forms
Rhythm of spoken German: chunking, pauses, discourse markers, fillers used skilfully
Collocational accuracy: choosing the verb a native would choose
Contemporary usage: trending words, youth language, neologisms, gender-inclusive language (debate and forms)
Tone control in writing: e-mail etiquette, Anrede and Grußformeln by context
Reading between the lines: implicature, subtext, politeness codes
Literary and philosophical canon you meet in conversation (Goethe, Schiller, Kafka, Brecht, Mann, Kant, Nietzsche)
Contemporary German-language film, TV, music, humour and podcasts
Political and social debates in Germany, Austria and Switzerland

Regional identity and mentality: Hesse, Bavaria, Saxony, the north, Vienna, Zurich
History and memory culture (Erinnerungskultur), 20th century to present
Mediate a text for a specific audience, adapting register, structure and level of detail
Mediate complex concepts, including from your own field, to non-specialists
